title: The Things Everyone Wants
author: Scott D. Clary
summary: The jobs and lifestyles everyone is told to pursue often deliver neither fulfillment nor the promised psychological rewards once attained. Sarah spent seven years pursuing venture capital, networking relentlessly, building the right relationships, and persisting through forty-three rejections before finally landing the position. Six months into the role, she realized the job she had invested years chasing was making her miserable, not because venture capital is inherently bad but because the competition and pursuit had become the actual reward, and obtaining the prize stripped away what made the chase meaningful. True fulfillment comes from discovering what you actually want rather than pursuing what everyone else wants you to want.
points: The pursuit often contains more psychological reward than the achievement; once the goal is attained, the absence of the chase leaves many feeling empty and unfulfilled.

Social pressure and external metrics shape what we pursue, leading many to spend years and significant effort chasing goals that don't actually align with their values or sources of genuine fulfillment.
Achievement without meaning becomes hollow, and prestige acquired through relentless pursuit of someone else's definition of success often fails to deliver promised satisfaction.
True fulfillment requires examining and articulating what you actually want rather than defaulting to what society, your industry, or your peers have determined should be desirable.
quotes: Sarah spent seven years trying to break into venture capital. She moved to San Francisco. Networked relentlessly. Did the right internships. Read all the right books. Followed all the right people. Built relationships with partners at every major firm. Got rejected forty-three times. Finally, on attempt forty-four, she got in.

Six months later, she realized the job she'd spent seven years chasing was making her miserable. The work was fine. The compensation was good. But the thing everyone told her was worth wanting turned out to be profoundly unrewarding.
Not because venture capital is bad. Because by the time she got there, the competition had ruined it. The thing that had driven her for seven years wasn't the job itself; it was the pursuit of it.

The things everyone wants, the things we see celebrated and admired, often fail to satisfy in the way we expect them to. The pursuit itself becomes the prize, and once you've attained it, the emptiness is deafening.
True fulfillment comes from discovering what you actually want rather than what the world says you should want.” Archived from Scott D. Clary Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
